doc.title: Vincent Pelote interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 25, 2017

chapter: Rutgers and the Institute of Jazz Studies
title: Rutgers Newark music major and Ed Berger's call to the Institute
summary: He meant to major in English but enrolled in music, fought for jazz in a classical program, and left substitute teaching for a cataloguing grant at the Institute.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: And this was at what school?

This was Rutgers University in Newark. Yeah. So I went over there because I got accepted to Rutgers. So I figured okay fine, this is good, I will go to Rutgers and be an English major. But anyway he talked to me and he said, “You know there’s a lot of things you could do with a music degree.” And he was trying to talk to me about becoming part of the department. And he gave me this sheet of paper that had all the different types of jobs you could get if you got a music degree. And I was floored. Because I figured the only thing you could do with music is play, and I didn’t think I was good enough to be a performer. And so I looked at it and said, “Hey, not bad.” So I signed up to be a music major. And I told him, I said, “I really don’t know that much about classical music but I love jazz. I mean if you guys don’t mind me being a jazz guy, okay.” And he was like, “Sure, no problem, come on in.” You know. So I did it and I don’t know, all through the four years that I was there, four and a half years, I was in this constant fight where, you know, they were doing the classical thing. In fact I remember for my audition to be in, I guess the choir, they wanted you to sing a song, and so they were all singing these © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
classical things. I chose “Moonlight Serenade.” That was my audition piece. Because I knew —

I taught this poor young lady to play piano behind me on this thing and I was terrible. I mean I am not a singer. I am horrible. And she put up with that. And today, we still talk about it today, sitting in the practice room, and she had to coach me into doing this. And another thing I did with the jazz thing is in the orchestration class we were given a little piece of music to orchestrate, and while they’re all doing classical things, I orchestrated a Duke Ellington thing. So every chance I got I tried to work that in, into my education, and it just never left me. It just stuck. So I settled on being a music ed teacher, because I figured all right, I would get out, I would probably get a stage band or a jazz band, a high school level thing, and I could do that. Because I didn’t want to be a vocal teacher. I didn’t want to do the vocal choir thing. I wanted to do a band thing. So I figured that’s going to be my thing. I was going to just be that. And maybe that’s where I’d be today if Ed Berger hadn’t called me and said, “Vinny, there’s a job at the Institute. We have a two year grant to catalogue sound recordings, and we need someone who knows something about jazz. We’ll teach you how to catalogue, but we just need the jazz expertise and I know you have it. Do you want to leave teaching and do this for two years.” I said, “Yes, take me away.” Because I’d been substitute teaching and it was like horrible, the kids were terrible, I couldn’t stand it anymore And I said, “I’ll take it. I’ll take it for two years and we’ll see what happens.” So I did. And it was the first time that anybody had done a catalogue project of that nature for jazz music on a national database. And that was OCLC at the time. That was the only national database that was really out there. So that’s how I got started. That’s really where the whole thing started. And I just never left. Because once the grant was out they applied for another one to do LPs. First it was 78s, then it was LPs, so I did that. And then after that we just sort of killed the whole thing and they realized, you know, Vinny knows more than just how to catalog sound recordings. He knows a lot about jazz. So they kept me on and just kept moving me from one thing to another.
